desc:
Given an array nums of positive integers and a positive integer ratio, count the index triples i < j < k such that nums[j] = nums[i] * ratio and nums[k] = nums[j] * ratio.

Triples are distinguished by position. The count can be huge (for ratio = 1 and an array of equal values it is C(n, 3)), so return it modulo 1,000,000,007.

For example, nums = [1, 2, 2, 4] and ratio = 2 give 2, and nums = [1, 1, 1, 1] with ratio = 1 gives 4.
hints: Checking all triples is O(n3). Try treating each element as the middle of a triple: how many valid left and right partners does it have?
For a middle value v you need earlier elements equal to v / ratio (if divisible) and later elements equal to v * ratio. Counting these with hash maps takes O(1) per element.

Single pass alternative: keep one[x] = how many times x has been seen, and two[x] = number of valid pairs (a, a * ratio) ending in value x. For each new value x: add two[x / ratio] to the answer, then add one[x / ratio] to two[x], then increment one[x].
editorial: Process the array left to right and maintain two maps. one[x] counts earlier occurrences of the value x; two[x] counts earlier pairs (i, j) with nums[j] = x and nums[i] = x / ratio. When a new element x arrives and x is divisible by ratio, every counted pair ending in x / ratio completes into a triple, so add two[x / ratio] to the answer.

The order of the three updates matters: first complete triples with the old two, then extend pairs with the old one, then record x itself. This also makes ratio = 1 work, since an element never pairs with itself. Time and space are O(n); only the final answer needs the modulus, because the intermediate pair counts stay below C(10,000, 2).
